The fragment's depth value must not be modified in the fragment shader [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the fragment's depth value must not be modified in the fragment shader. Source [S1] explicitly states in the notes and the main text: 'The early z-test is only enabled if all other per-fragment tests are disabled and the fragment's depth value is not modified in the shader.' Since the claim accurately reflects this condition described in the evidence, the verdict is supported.

Early Z-Test Acceleration is a hardware optimization applied before the fragment shader executes for a particular fragment to avoid shader execution, enabling the fragment processor to immediately process the next incoming fragment [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that Early Z-Test Acceleration is a hardware optimization applied before the fragment shader executes to avoid shader execution, enabling the processor to move to the next fragment. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the passage: 'The essential mechanism... is the early z-test. It is applied before the shader program is executed for a particular fragment, and it can be used to avoid the execution thus enabling a fragment processor to process the next incoming fragment.' The notes also corroborate this description.

*   Depth modification in the shader disables the early z-test, forcing fallback to standard execution order [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that depth modification in the shader disables the early z-test. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'The early z-test, however, is only enabled if all other per-fragment tests are disabled and the fragments depth value is not modified in the shader.' This implies that if the depth value is modified, the early z-test is not enabled (i.e., it is disabled), forcing the system to proceed with standard execution (executing the shader). Therefore, the evidence supports the claim.

Unlike software-based checks that still invoke the shader, this method discards occluded fragments at the hardware level, yielding performance gains of up to a factor of 3 for typical volumetric datasets on hardware such as the ATI 9700 [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method discards occluded fragments at the hardware level (unlike software-based checks that invoke the shader), yielding performance gains of up to a factor of 3 for typical volumetric datasets on hardware such as the ATI 9700. All specific facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

*   Do not use if the volume is the first object rendered or if the shader requires depth modification [S1, unofficial].

The evidence supports the part of the claim regarding 'shader requires depth modification' (S1 states: 'the early z-test... is only enabled if... the fragments depth value is not modified in the shader'). However, the evidence does not support the part of the claim regarding 'if the volume is the first object rendered'. In fact, the evidence suggests the opposite or a different condition: it states that a speedup is perceived when 'depth values have been written in the first pass' (implying an object was rendered before the volume to occlude it), rather than the volume being the first object. The claim's condition about being the first object is not supported by the text.
